title: She Leapt 6.88 Metres and Ended a 22-Year Wait. Then the High Jumper Made History Too.
excerpt: Ancy Sojan shattered Anju Bobby George's iconic long jump national record, and Sarvesh Kushare became the first Indian to clear 2.30 metres — both at the Inter-State Championships in Bhubaneswar on Saturday.
body:
For more than two decades, Anju Bobby George's 6.83-metre leap at the 2004 Athens Olympics had stood as the ceiling for Indian women's long jump. Every season, it survived. Athletes came close, retreated, moved on. The record outlasted coaching changes, federation squabbles, and an entire generation of jumpers who grew up watching replays of the moment that made George the first Indian to medal at a World Championships in track and field.

On Saturday evening at the Kalinga Stadium in Bhubaneswar, Kerala's Ancy Sojan finally brought it down.

Her fifth-attempt leap of 6.88 metres — five centimetres beyond George's mark — rewrote a record that predates the iPhone, YouTube, and any social media platform the Indian diaspora now scrolls through for sports news. The 25-year-old Indian Navy Chief Petty Officer signalled her intent from the very first jump, opening with 6.73 metres before a no-mark on her second attempt and marks of 6.67 and 6.72 on her third and fourth. When the electronic scoreboard flashed 6.88 on her penultimate effort, Sojan had her answer.

"My goal today was a personal best of 6.75m," Sojan said afterward, still processing a leap well beyond her own expectations. She closed the night with a 6.69-metre final jump — itself proof of her consistency across the series. "My father wanted someone in the family to be a national record holder. The gold medal will be a precious gift to him."

## The Comeback Behind the Record

Sojan's path to the record has not been linear. A silver medallist at the Hangzhou Asian Games and at the 2025 Asian Athletics Championships, she spent much of last year struggling with health issues that forced an extended break from competition. "It was mentally and physically challenging," she said. "I'm happy to have made a comeback — that too ahead of the Aichi Nagoya Asian Games starting September 19."

She set a personal best of 6.75 metres at the Federation Cup in Ranchi just four weeks ago, signalling that the record was within reach. Saturday's performance confirmed it.

The woman whose record she eclipsed could not have been more gracious. In an interview with RevSportz, Anju Bobby George said she had been expecting it. "At last, after 22 years, it's happened," George said. "Every other event was improving, and my event was standing at the same place. I am happy that someone came and broke my record — and that too Ancy, from Kerala. I was keeping in my mind that if somebody broke my record, it should be a clean athlete. And she is so consistent throughout the years."

George also named Shaili Singh as another future contender, noting that "these two athletes are our future."

## The Army Man Who Cleared 2.31

![Sarvesh Kushare competing in the high jump](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/5/5c/Sarvesh_Kushare.jpg)

If Sojan's record felt like a long-awaited exhale, the one that followed in the men's high jump felt like a crescendo. Maharashtra's Sarvesh Kushare cleared 2.31 metres on his third attempt, breaking Tejaswin Shankar's eight-year-old national mark of 2.29 metres and becoming the first Indian man to officially clear the 2.30-metre barrier.

"I was feeling good," the 31-year-old Indian Army Naib Subedar said. "I got a big boost when I cleared 2.27m. Thereafter, I pushed and made an attempt to break the national record." He then set the bar at 2.35 metres — territory that would place him among Asia's absolute elite — but two attempts at that height came up short.

Kushare's journey from a makeshift training pit in Deogaon village near Nashik — stuffed with corn husks, agricultural waste, and old clothing — to an Olympic start in Paris and a historic sixth-place finish at the 2025 World Championships in Tokyo has become one of Indian athletics' most compelling narratives. His father had wanted him to become a civil engineer. The son had other plans.

The Inter-State Championships, now in their 65th edition, continued to deliver across the board on Day 4. Yoonus Shah of Uttar Pradesh erased Bahadur Prasad's 1500m meet record with a time of 3:37.55 seconds. Karnataka's Yashas P improved his own 400m hurdles meet record to 49.14 seconds, matching Tamil Nadu's Santhosh T to the hundredth. And in the shot put, Punjab's Karanveer Singh launched a throw of 20.49 metres to lead a trio of 20-metre-plus efforts.

## What It Means for the Diaspora

For NRIs watching from afar, both records carry a familiar texture: Indian athletes chipping away at barriers long assumed permanent, small-town determination meeting the global stage at precisely the right moment. Beyond the numbers, both Sojan and Kushare have punched their tickets for the Aichi Nagoya Asian Games in September. The real question now becomes whether Saturday's leaps in Bhubaneswar were the peak — or just the start of something higher.
